This means we assume the user can perform some other manual steps such as generating and distributing certs and managing API keys. We support multiple concurrent users accessing the same job, but do not take care for very high scalability on this service via load balancing or throttling in this scope.
+
+The general approach is to split the key functions of this service between the library, API, and client.
+- The libary will manage basic job functions as well as the bulk of the output streaming logic to allow concurrent clients to view job output.
+- The API adds authentication and authorization on top of the library and provides a gRPC interface to the library. For this prototype, authorization is kept to a simple API key model with one "admin" key and general users being restricted to the jobs they started.
+- The client is a simple command line that calls our API using pre-generated API keys. Worker output is streamed as is from the server down to the client.
+
+## Library
+
+**Library requirements and limitations**:
+ - Start and stop jobs which are command line processes and allow users to immediately read job output as well as query job output.
+ - Multiple clients can concurrently read the output of the same job.
+- Limitations:
+  - Clients running or stopping the same job are treated as first come first serve. Clients expecting to run multiple instances of the same job should provide unique job ids.
+  - It is not currently planned to support jobs with very large output.
+  - No safety considerations around running processes - no checking for malicious processes or processes which may interfere with other processes or the system. Launched processes are considered black boxes.
+
+
+**Output streaming**:
+Go standard library already provides methods to start and stop system commands while retrieving their output. To support multiple concurrent readers of the same job and to allow clients to both immediately get output and resume reading from the client’s last known read output, we wrap the job output with in-memory buffering. We support a maximum output buffer size for jobs with very large output. The implementation should be flexible enough that potential future work could write some of the buffer to disk or an external object store if we wanted to store very large amounts of output.
+
+
+**Library methods**:
+- `createJobRunner(JobRunnerSpec)` creates a job runner instance with configuration such as default job timeouts and max job output buffer size (output limited to last N bytes)  if any
+- All other methods are on the `JobRunner`.
+ - `start(JobId, JobSpec)` launchs a job and returns output streams for stdout and stderr or error. Output streams are essentially io.Reader implementations wrapping our internal job output pipes and stored job output.
+ - `stop(JobId)` stops a job, which should result in any of our internal listeners
+ - `status(JobId)` returns basic information about the job without the output -  job name, job spec, if currently still running, and when the job started.
+ - `output(JobId, OutputMode, (optional) Cursor)` returns an implementation of `io.Reader` of job output optionally starting an existing cursor, OutputMode for which outputs to capture - stdout or stderr.
+Cursor can be a number of bytes in to start reading from or number of bytes from the end (roughly, with no guarantees on exact match if the job is still generating output). 
+ - Library public data structures (protobufs shared with API):
+`JobName` - identifier of job as `byte[]`
+`JobSpec` - command to run, timeout for job running time, ttl for maintaining job information after the job is done - ie how long after the job finishes can you retrieve the job output?
+
+**General flow of job lifecycle**:
+The above generally covers library functions. To be more specific, this is an example workflow:
+1. User requests starting a job giving it a name and job spec.
+2. Check against known running jobs using the given JobName, if already running return a `JobAlreadyRunning` error.
+Create a Job structure which will store any in memory information regarding the job - `JobId`, `JobSpec`, current status, and the io.Reader of the job output.
+3. Launch the job by starting the command line and capturing all output for the reader (implemented by primarily wrapping os.exec functions), without waiting for completion. Immediately attach a listener that will wait for the job to finish and update metadata on the job’s running status.
+4. Create another listener which follows the job’s output streams for an internal job reader which can be wrapped to provide multiple concurrent users access to the job output (more reader details below)
+5. Return an output reader for the job.
+6. User requests status partway through a job run:
+`status(JobId)` will simply query the in-memory store of jobs and return the metadata we know about the job.
+`output(JobId, OutputMode, (optional) Cursor)` will retrieve a Reader for the job with the output modes requested by wrapping our internal reader.
+7. User requests job to stop:
+stop(JobName) checks if the job is already stopped and will use os.exec methods to stop the job. Our in memory Job representation will update to reflect the job is now stopped.
+8. Job stops naturally:
+Our listeners should stop on their own, and job output streams will stop. Job status will be updated to stopped. Output will be saved until the ttl for job output.
+9. Job hits its timeout:
+We stop the job forcefully also shutting down any still active listeners.
+
+
+## API
+
+API methods broadly follow the library with the addition of mTLS authentication and a very simple authorization scheme.
+- `createKey()` creates an API key (crypto/rand generated random base64 string).
+- Job commands mirror library with `start(Context, JobId, JobSpec)`, `stop(Context, JobId)`, etc. API keys will be pulled off of contexts for authorization.
+- Job output takes the library’s provided reader and wraps it into a gRPC stream of bytes.
